title: HFrEF: judging volume and using diuretics

source.citation: Gauer RL, Rifaat A, Foulkrod AM. Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction: Medical Management. Am Fam Physician. 2025;112(2):131-145.

questions.q: Which bedside finding has the highest positive likelihood ratio for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
questions.why: Its LR+ is only 2.18, which is why the article calls clinical assessment of volume unreliable, and it is hard to judge in obese patients.

questions.q: What is the specificity of bilateral leg oedema for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema?
questions.why: Its sensitivity is 94%, so its absence is somewhat reassuring, but its presence has too many other causes to mean much.

questions.q: Which sign is highly specific but very insensitive for pulmonary oedema?
questions.why: Rales are 90% specific but 13% sensitive, and can be absent altogether in chronic heart failure.

questions.q: Which bedside test is more accurate than chest radiography or natriuretic peptides for acute heart failure?
questions.a: Point-of-care ultrasound of the inferior vena cava and lungs
questions.why: In a meta-analysis, lung ultrasound identified 15 more cases of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema per 100 dyspnoeic patients than chest radiography.

questions.q: On point-of-care ultrasound the inferior vena cava measures 2.5 cm and collapses less than 50% on sniff. What does this indicate?
questions.why: The normal pattern is under 2.1 cm with more than 50% collapse; the measurement is unreliable when intrathoracic pressure is raised, as with ascites, ileus or mechanical ventilation.

questions.q: How many B-lines on lung ultrasound define interstitial oedema?
questions.a: More than three in more than two bilateral intercostal spaces
d: More than one in a single space
questions.why: B-lines are vertical comet tails from oedematous interlobular septa; they also appear in noncardiac lung disease, so pairing them with a natriuretic peptide raises specificity to 90%.

questions.q: Below what BNP level is heart failure effectively excluded?
questions.why: Its negative likelihood ratio is 0.08; NT-proBNP under 300 pg/mL does the same job with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.02.

questions.q: Which conditions raise natriuretic peptides in the absence of heart failure?
questions.why: Obesity does the opposite: levels run disproportionately low, so a normal value in an obese patient is less reassuring.

questions.q: Which loop diuretic is preferred first line for congestion in HFrEF?
questions.why: Torsemide and bumetanide have better oral bioavailability and are the usual alternatives when furosemide fails; ethacrynic acid is kept for sulfonamide hypersensitivity.

questions.q: What is the usual starting dose of oral furosemide for new outpatient heart failure?
questions.why: Higher doses are needed in advanced heart failure and kidney disease; the usual ceiling beyond which extra diuresis is minimal is 80 mg twice daily.

questions.q: For a patient already on oral furosemide who is admitted with decompensation, how does the initial intravenous dose relate to the oral dose?
questions.a: Up to twice the oral dose
d: A quarter of the oral dose
The same as the oral dose
options: A quarter of the oral dose
The same as the oral dose
Up to twice the oral dose
questions.why: Diuretic-naive patients start at 20 to 40 mg intravenously. Furosemide's intravenous to oral ratio is 1:2, unlike torsemide and bumetanide at 1:1.

questions.q: High-dose loop diuretic is failing to decongest a patient. Which agents are appropriate to add?
questions.why: Kidney function and electrolytes need close monitoring on combined diuretics; this is also the point to consider changing the loop diuretic itself.

questions.q: During effective diuresis, what creatinine rise is associated with better outcomes rather than harm?
questions.why: A doubling, or a rise over 1 mg/dL, should prompt a search for another cause of kidney dysfunction, especially if the patient stays congested with poor urine output.

questions.q: What weight gain should prompt a patient to take an extra dose of furosemide?
questions.a: 3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
options: 3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week
questions.why: The extra dose is 20 to 40 mg, and the underlying principle is the lowest diuretic dose that holds the dry weight.

questions.q: Which findings indicate that diuresis is working?
questions.why: None of them alone predicts that pulmonary decongestion is complete, which is where bedside ultrasound earns its place.
